answers.implementation_then_now: 2023: the US State Department 2022 report found that MTSS enforced minimum wage and overtime effectively in San José and the formal sector, but less so in rural areas with many migrants. It also found employers used deportation threats to withhold Nicaraguan migrants' wages. 2026: the 2023 and 2024 reports repeat the same urban/rural enforcement gap. The ASIDEHU study (Sept. 2024, reported by 100% Noticias) found 88% of Nicaraguan respondents earned below the minimum wage. The pattern is unchanged: the law is honoured in the formal sector, with systematic gaps in agriculture.

answers.implementation_then_now: No source documents a pattern of DGME refusing change-of-employer applications, either around 2022 or in 2023-2025. The documented problem in both periods is the large share of migrants working without authorisation in agriculture, where enforcement is weak (US State Dept 2022, 2023 and 2024 reports). No shift is documented. The rating is partly inferred, because no source covers change-of-employer processing as such.

answers.implementation_then_now: 2023: the US State Dept 2022 report found working-hour, overtime and OSH laws enforced effectively mainly in San José and the formal sector. It found weaker enforcement in rural areas with many migrants, and reported that migrant pineapple workers were exposed to hazardous chemicals without training. 2026: the 2023 and 2024 reports repeat these findings almost verbatim and add that agricultural migrants are hired on short-term contracts through intermediaries and are more exposed to exploitation. Inspectors cannot impose sanctions themselves, and court cases are slow. No shift is documented. Much of this evidence concerns agricultural and irregular workers rather than permit holders.

answers.implementation_then_now: 2023: the US State Dept 2022 report records discrimination against Nicaraguan migrant workers, employers using deportation threats, and a UN independent expert's warning of rising xenophobic hate speech. MTSS recorded no nationality or ethnicity discrimination cases (five cases, all disability or gender). 2026: the 2023 State Dept report notes xenophobia among service providers. The 2025 UN/COES study (via 100% Noticias) counted 326,326 xenophobic posts between June 2024 and May 2025. The ASIDEHU 2024 study found 90% of Nicaraguans interviewed had experienced xenophobia, including at work. The pattern of weak enforcement is the same in both periods.
